## 1. Repository Setup and Branching Strategy

Bounty repositories that rely on automated validation pipelines require strict adherence to Git hygiene and directory conventions. The first step is to fork `Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties` directly from the GitHub interface, then clone the forked repository to a local development environment using `git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/rustchain-bounties.git`. Once cloned, initialize the upstream remote to maintain synchronization with the canonical repository: `git remote add upstream https://github.com/Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties.git`. This dual-remote configuration prevents stale-state errors when the bounty maintainer updates validation schemas or merges prior submissions.

Create an isolated feature branch using the exact naming convention specified in the issue tracker: `git checkout -b feature/bottube-review-[handle]`, where `[handle]` is replaced with your ToolPilot.ai username or wallet identifier. Isolated branching is non-negotiable in high-throughput bounty repos; it prevents cross-contamination of markdown files, ensures linear commit history, and allows the auto-submit bot to parse PR boundaries without triggering merge conflict warnings. Before writing any content, navigate to the submission directory. Most RustChain-style bounty repos store review artifacts under `contrib/reviews/` or `submissions/toolpilot/`. If a template exists (commonly named `TEMPLATE_review.md` or `_schema_example.md`), copy it into your branch and rename it according to the required slug format, typically `bottube-[handle].md`. Verify file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM, as GitHub Actions YAML parsers frequently reject malformed headers.

**Takeaway:** A cleanly branched, upstream-synced repository structure with correctly named markdown artifacts is the prerequisite for passing CI validation; deviations trigger immediate bot rejections before human review occurs.
